calc.metodo_titulo: How this number is worked out
calc.metodo_p1: There is no invented coefficient table. The calculator takes the published items of the section you pick in that country's catalog, multiplies each one by your quantity and shows every result. The range comes from the catalog itself: the low is the cheapest item in the section, the high is the most expensive one (standard tile versus large-format porcelain, for example).
calc.metodo_p2: The materials, labour and equipment split also comes from each item's real cost breakdown, weighted by amount. That is what tells you whether the job is material-heavy or crew-hour-heavy, which is the difference between work that leaves a margin and work that does not.
calc.incluye_titulo: What it includes and what it leaves out
calc.incluye1: Includes the direct cost of the item: materials, labour and equipment, with their yields.
calc.incluye2: Includes the indirect and complementary costs the catalog folds into the unit price.
calc.incluye3: Excludes tax: it is applied on the taxable base when you build the estimate.
calc.incluye4: Excludes your profit, site-wide preliminaries and any preparation work that is not part of the item.
calc.metodo_p3: A catalog unit price is a defensible starting point, not a closed offer: it changes by city, by supplier and by site access. Adjust it with your own data before you sign.

mo.intro: Catalog data for {pais}: {n} trades with their hourly cost in {moneda}, with each trade's weight in the catalog items and the revision date ({mes}).
mo.lectura_titulo: How to read hourly labour rates in {pais}
mo.lectura1: The most expensive hour in the catalog is {caro}, at {caro_txt}, and the cheapest is {barato}, at {barato_txt}. The gap is not arbitrary: the specialist trade charges more per hour, but the item that uses it usually carries fewer hours per unit of work, so the price per square metre does not rise by the same amount.
mo.lectura2: The weight column tells you how many catalog items each trade appears in. That is the most honest way to sort the table: what comes first is what actually holds a job together (the helper crew is on almost every item), not what sounds most technical.
mo.lectura3: When several trades show the same figure it is because that market's catalog uses one reference rate for that level. Where they really separate is in the yield: two trades with the same hourly cost can produce very different amounts of work per day, and that is what moves the unit price of the item.
mo.como1: This is not a survey or a copied wage table. These are the labour resources the catalog for {pais} itself uses to build its unit prices: the {total} published items are walked, hours are grouped by trade and their cost is averaged. The current catalog revision is {mes}.
mo.como2: It includes the crew cost to the contractor (wages and employer charges), exactly as it enters each item's cost breakdown.
mo.como3: It excludes your profit, the job's indirect costs and site equipment. To turn it into an estimate you still have to add those.
mo.como4: It excludes tax: that is applied on the taxable base when you build the estimate, on top of the cost price in {moneda}.
mo.como5: It is a market reference cost. A tradesman in a city, on an industrial estate and in a rural area does not cost the same, and the catalog does not pretend to know your case: it gives you the base to adjust.

cmp.intro: {n} construction items sharing the same code in {n_mercados} markets, compared in USD at the {fecha} exchange rate. Index 100 = international median.
cmp.intro_cap: The {n} items in “{capitulo}” that share the same code in {n_mercados} markets, compared in USD at the {fecha} exchange rate. Index 100 = international median.
cmp.tabla_caption: Catalog price level by market, across {n} identical items
cmp.lectura1: Of the {n} published markets, {mayor} has the most expensive catalog and {menor} the cheapest for exactly the same items. The gap between them is not a small percentage: it is a multiple.
cmp.lectura2: The index does not measure the cost of living, it measures what construction costs according to each country's catalog. Three things mix in there: local material and labour cost, crew productivity and the exchange rate. When a market is out of line, one of the three is behind it.
cmp.lectura3: The comparison uses the median rather than the mean: one badly loaded price in a single market must not move the other 21. That is also why each country's index is the median of its ratios rather than an average of prices.
cmp.partidas_titulo: The items whose price changes most between countries
cmp.partidas_texto: These are not the most expensive ones, they are the ones that spread widest between the cheapest and the most expensive market. That is where you see which work depends on local cost and which on imported material.
cmp.como1: The {n} items that share the exact same code in all {n_mercados} catalogs are taken, so it is the same work unit everywhere. Lump-sum items are excluded because they cannot be compared per unit.
cmp.como2: Every price is converted to metric units (US square feet and cubic yards are converted) and to USD at the frozen reference rate dated {fecha}. That date is the exchange rate date, not the catalog date: each market has its own and it is shown on its own page.
cmp.como3: For each item the median of the 22 market prices is calculated. A market's index is the median of its ratios against those medians, times 100.
cmp.como4: Everything comes from the published catalog. If a market revises its prices, its index changes on its own: there is no hand-written table that goes stale.
